We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.

title: A Plan or an Adversarial Example? A Round-Trip Check for Latent World Models
summary: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.

title: Portable Active Recovery under Timed and Position-Dependent Visual Outages
summary: When a camera blackout depends on physical position rather than elapsed time, stable hovering prevents visual recovery and mission completion. On stereo visual-inertial quadrotors without external localization, an exogenous timed blackout and an endogenous position-dependent dark zone appear identical at loss onset yet require opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93/96 timed blackouts but 0/96 spatial outages (13 hard failures), whereas blind continuation traverses many spatial zones yet fails heavily during timed blackouts. We formulate visual-outage recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and introduce a portable recovery module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller with zero retraining. Using deployable telemetry alone, the module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional gated prior-map branch. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark (1,920 flights), our full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition completion, outperforming development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] and exceeding all six external baselines after Bonferroni correction. Attached without retraining to SimpleFlight, the module lifts worst-condition completion by +17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0x/1.25x speeds, 0/80 hard failures). Trace diagnostics reveal that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition asymmetry at vision return -- not blind IMU drift suppression - and uncover a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on 72 held-out EuRoC windows.

title: CoEvoBench: Can LLMs Drive Recursive Co-Evolution of Agentic Systems?
summary: The performance of an LLM agent depends on both its model and its harness, the code that mediates its interaction with tools and environments. Can LLM researchers drive this co-evolution as a recursive improvement process, deciding round after round which component to change when each change alters the value of the other? Existing benchmarks evaluate post-training or data research with the harness out of scope, or harness optimization with the model fixed, leaving this joint decision unmeasured. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs as researchers co-evolving the model and harness of a target agent across five agentic domains. Researchers start from a common base model and initial harness, train and revise within a 24-hour budget, and submit a model-harness pair that is scored on separate test tasks. Across five frontier researchers, the strongest closes more than four fifths of the gap to an instruction-tuned reference system, and co-evolution succeeds on interaction tasks but rarely on long-horizon coding. These results suggest that current LLMs can make a strong first improvement, but cannot yet turn feedback from an improved system into the next one. CoEvoBench provides a controlled testbed for measuring the research capabilities that recursive co-evolution requires.

title: Federated and Balanced $k$-means: Communication Efficiency, Privacy, and Heterogeneity
summary: Collaborating on data across organizations in healthcare and finance demands methods that preserve privacy while enabling effective analysis. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) facilitates clustering across data where different parties hold different features of the same entities without sharing raw data. However, existing VFL clustering methods suffer from two key limitations: vulnerability to information leakage and the creation of imbalanced clusters. To address these limitations, we propose Fabric, a balanced and privacy-preserving federated $k$-means algorithm. Our method decomposes the balanced clustering problem into independent subproblems for each client, using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to efficiently handle the balance constraints. Under the semi-honest model, Fabric provides provable privacy guarantees by injecting calibrated noise into local objective evaluations. Extensive evaluations on ten real-world datasets show that Fabric achieves a superior utility-privacy trade-off compared with state-of-the-art methods and converges faster. Specifically, Fabric reduces SSE by 29.1\% on average and improves balance performance by 1.41$\times$, while being 26$\times$ faster on average.

title: RemoteEvolver: Expanding Earth Observation Capabilities through Agent Harness Evolution
summary: We are interested in developing a continually self-improving remote sensing agentic system. It should identify and address its capability gaps, retaining the resulting improvements to enhance performance on subsequent tasks. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed toolsets and confine their experience accumulation to re-orchestrating predefined capabilities, constraining both capability expansion and the transfer of improvements across tasks. As the infrastructure for agentic systems, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. These resources can therefore be updated and reused across tasks without additional post-training. Based on these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, an external harness for remote sensing agents that drives tool and workflow evolution through execution feedback. With the base model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing specialized tools on demand and distills verified successful execution experience from individual tasks into agent skills that can be reused across tasks. The acquired tools and accumulated skills jointly support planning and execution on subsequent tasks. Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench show that RemoteEvolver achieves average accuracy gains of 8.18 and 23.86 percentage points over its initial state when tools are fully available and partially missing. Under the same settings, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6.77 and 17.10 percentage points, respectively.

title: Recurrent Amplification and Exact Nonexpansiveness Criteria for Query-Driven Erasure
summary: The Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) augments a rank-one linear attention update with a key-orthogonal query component. Under scalar decay, this correction leaves the eigenvalues of each homogeneous state transition unchanged, while the propagation of an initial perturbation depends on the ordered product of these transitions. We construct a periodic token sequence with fixed key and query projections for which every one-step spectral radius is below one but the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one. The same construction yields a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay, we derive a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness that can be evaluated in $O(d)$ time. The test agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators evaluated. In a counterfactual replay of a selected head of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence increased from 0.99938 to 1.3977 with the feature and checkpoint gate trajectories held fixed.

title: Reliable Behavior Discovery via False Discovery Rate Control
summary: Reliable methods for discovering behavior patterns in large generative models are increasingly essential as models become both more complex and capable. We formalize behavior discovery as a problem class of interest and highlight the task of controlling false discovery rate (FDR) as crucial for guaranteeing reliability in behavior discovery. Building upon the multiple hypothesis testing literature, we propose DISCO (Discovery through Iterative Search with COarsened $e$-processes), a method which provably controls FDR in behavior discovery under mild conditions. DISCO improves power over previous related eBH-based approaches by allowing for adaptivity to a data-dependent number of hypotheses to be tested. We demonstrate empirically that DISCO controls FDR with higher power than comparable approaches on both synthetic data and a novel empirical evaluation of FDR-controlling methods in settings where large generative models act as both discovery engines and targets. Code is available at https://github.com/google-deepmind/disco .

title: One state, many questions: Opsis gives a frontier model typed eyes for pathology
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 12 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/gezhixuan/opsis
summary: A synoptic pathology report is a checklist of questions with fixed answer sets, many composed from others. Pathology foundation models answer them accurately with one classifier trained with labels for each, and frontier language models, which compose freely, cannot fit a slide of fourteen thousand tiles in their context. On 189 breast report questions, frontier models that read a written description of the slide or look at a thumbnail and tiles of it answer at 0.50 to 0.66, below the majority class at 0.67. A description is written before the question is known, and a look covers a handful of tiles. We present Opsis, which lets the model ask instead: a typed question interface on a frozen pathology encoder. A slide is encoded once, a question names an operator, arguments and candidates given at runtime, and the answer is a probability over the candidates. We build it as a 10 M parameter decoder on frozen Virchow2 tokens (Opsis-S) and inside Qwen3-VL-8B (Opsis-V). Asking Opsis-S, four frontier models answer the breast questions at 0.78 to 0.79, and on 3,797 pan cancer questions asking is 8.6 points above reading. On 995 composite questions that Opsis-S was never trained on, a frontier model composing its answers reaches 0.76, against 0.69 when it looks at the slide and 0.78 for ABMIL trained on each composite. On a pan cancer question set over 10,712 TCGA slides, one Opsis-S decoder matches linear probes trained per question on TITAN and PRISM2 embeddings (average accuracy 0.69 against 0.70 and 0.68). Opsis-S also separates CAMELYON16 metastases without training on that cohort (AUROC 0.86) and localises necrosis from report labels alone (tile AUROC 0.93).

title: EgoSurgHands: An Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Dataset & Benchmark for Open Surgery Training
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code, dataset, and benchmark leaderboard available at https://egosurghands.github.io
summary: Surgical skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration all benefit from 3D tracking of the surgeon's hands, yet no surgical dataset offers real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose. We introduce EgoSurgHands, a benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels combine sensor-fused pseudo-ground truth, human cross-review of every frame, surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an independent multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18\% and 40\% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1\% of evaluation rows. As a baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://egosurghands.github.io

title: Reasoning in Two Dimensions: Quantifying Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness and Efficiency
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning exposes intermediate steps, but a correct answer does not establish that an LLM relies on the dependence expressed by those steps or reasons efficiently. We operationalize CoT faithfulness and efficiency within a common framework. Specifically, we represent a CoT as a semantic reasoning graph and decompose the model's predictive dependence along two complementary axes: dependence explained by semantic support versus additional reasoning history, and dependence allocated to answer-reaching versus off-path reasoning. This decomposition yields global and step-level measures of unfaithfulness and inefficiency. Controlled interventions show that the proposed metrics respond to hidden dependence and induced off-path reasoning as intended. Across mathematical and multi-hop reasoning tasks, answer-level unfaithfulness is consistently associated with greater predictive uncertainty, whereas both unfaithfulness and inefficiency exhibit weak or inconsistent associations with answer correctness. We further derive theoretically grounded, graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that improve the targeted reasoning properties without directly optimizing the computationally expensive metrics or compromising answer accuracy. Results indicate that accuracy and brevity provide incomplete assessments of reasoning quality: reliable CoT evaluation should also consider whether the LLM's predictive dependence is faithfully represented and efficiently allocated.

title: UDA-Restoration: Bridging Unsupervised Domain Adaptation and Multi-Degradation Denoising for Enhanced AV Semantic Segmentation
summary: Autonomous vehicles rely heavily on vision-based perception systems for safe navigation and decision-making. Adverse weather conditions, sensor noise, moving artifacts and illumination changes, however, often degrade the image quality and hence reduce perception performance. This paper introduces a diffusion-guided unsupervised domain adaptation algorithm for autonomous driving environments, namely UDA-Restoration, which is designed to enhance and denoise images. The proposed method follows the paradigm of Noise-Space Domain Adaptation (Noise-DA), which is based on multi-source degradation learning and diffusion-guided adaptation that spans across synthetic and real-world degradations. The framework has been extensively tested and shown to restore image quality and to be robust to unseen degradation scenarios, such as snow, haze, sensor distortions, and more. The quantitative results indicate that Noise-DA outperforms the evaluated self-supervised and unsupervised baselines while matching the best supervised restoration performance. In addition, semantic segmentation experiments show that the performance of downstream perception tasks is directly improved by better image restoration. The outcomes show the promise of unsupervised domain adaptation based on diffusion as a powerful and scalable method for image restoration tasks in autonomous driving systems under various environments.

title: PIU-CR: Physics-Informed Deep Unfolding with SAR-Optical Image Fusion for Cloud Removal
summary: Multi-modal cloud removal exploits complementary optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images to restore cloud-degraded remote sensing images. Most existing methods rely on black-box, data-driven architectures with limited interpretability of cross-modal interactions. Although some attempts introduce physical priors into networks, their oversimplified formulations fail to faithfully characterize the underlying physical imaging process and the networks remain loosely coupled with optimization variables. To address these issues, we propose a physics-informed deep unfolding network for cloud removal via optical-SAR image fusion, termed as PIU-CR. We first formulate cloud removal as a physics-informed optimization problem. Specifically, we fundamentally ground the optimization in the physical imaging mechanism of cloud degradation by embedding the atmospheric scattering model into the data fidelity term. Then, the regularization terms establish an explicit cross-modal interaction mechanism, overcoming the single-modal information scarcity and the obscure, uninterpretable interactions in black-box models. They are dedicated to SAR-guided structure and spectral regularization, jointly introducing cross-modal structural feature alignment and coordinated spectral consistency constraints. The resulting optimization problem is then unfolded into a multi-stage neural network with dedicated structure and spectral branches. Each stage corresponds to an explicit optimization iteration step, enabling interpretable and effective reconstruction process. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Fgq188/PIU_CR.

title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
summary: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.

title: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation
summary: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.

title: ORION: Exact Canonical-State Supervision for Systematic Generalization in Transformers
summary: Autoregressive Transformers generally fail on out-of-distribution reasoning due to two primary reasons: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep execution steps. We introduce ORION, a framework that supervises exact canonical execution states via auxiliary heads to anchor latent trajectories to valid computational manifolds. Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial shows that RoPE and ORION address orthogonal axes. RoPE recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%). Moreover, their combination complementarily achieves strict additive gain in joint length-depth extrapolation, while either method alone offers near satisfactory results. Negative controls confirm that the gain depends strictly on exact canonical alignment; hashed state statistics fail to constrain depth extrapolation.

title: Auditing and Adapting kNNGuard for Long-Context Prompts
summary: Training-free activation guardrails such as kNNGuard score prompts by comparing last-token LLM hidden states (the Layer Ensemble branch, kNNGuard LE) and sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Embedding-kNN) against a small reference bank (50 examples per class), combining the two branches into a Fused Ensemble (kNNGuard FE). While effective on short inputs (up to 256 tokens), standard kNNGuard degrades substantially on long inputs (over 1000 tokens): averaged across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it, kNNGuard LE AUROC drops from 0.742 (0.777 and 0.706) to 0.554 (0.587 and 0.521) on Content Harm Moderation (Aegis-2.0), and from 0.994 (0.995 and 0.992) to 0.556 (0.598 and 0.513) on RAG Hallucination Detection (HaluBench). We trace this degradation to three causes: (1) hidden-state drift as sequence length increases, (2) hard 256-token truncation in MiniLM, and (3) signal dilution when a long document is compressed into a single final-token vector. We then evaluate three training-free adaptations: a Length-Routed Dual Bank, a long-context embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), and Strided Window Pooling across intermediate token positions. On Content Harm Moderation, dual-bank routing and strided window pooling raise long-context kNNGuard LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 (+0.274 AUROC) and fused kNNGuard FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886 (+0.164 AUROC) with no latency overhead from bank routing. On RAG Hallucination Detection, where the guardrail must verify logical consistency between a generated answer and a retrieved passage, sentence-embedding kNN remains near random chance across all lengths, while length-matched LLM hidden states (kNNGuard LE) recover medium-length detection (AUROC = 0.853) but remain limited on over-1000-token passages (AUROC = 0.607) due to final-token dilution over long contexts.

title: Accelerating Muon with Spectral Residual Correction
summary: Muon constructs matrix updates by applying a matrix-sign transformation to momentum. A common route to accelerating Muon is to modify the gradient or momentum before this transformation. We explore a complementary direction: refining the parameter step while retaining Muon's momentum recursion. Derived from the parameter subproblem of the ADMM-Inspired Momentum framework, AIMuon uses the gradient--momentum residual to correct the tentative spectral step. The residual undergoes a separate matrix-sign transformation, while spectral--nuclear duality determines the relative weighting of the momentum and residual directions. In practice, both directions are approximated with Newton--Schulz iterations and their combination is rescaled to match Muon's update magnitude. We establish a stochastic stationarity bound for the corresponding exact iteration. On GPT-2-small, GPT-2-medium, and Qwen3-0.6B, AIMuon reaches Muon's final validation loss with 8.98\%, 10.05\%, and 6.49\% fewer optimization steps, respectively, while achieving lower final validation loss than Muon, Muon-Nesterov, and MONA.

title: Hindsight Forcing: Learning Better History from the Future in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
summary: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables real-time streaming generation, with each generated chunk serving as historical context for subsequent generation. To avoid the memory explosion of backpropagation through time, previous self-rollout methods typically truncate cross-chunk gradients or detach historical latents. As a result, earlier denoising computations receive no downstream feedback through the generated history on how to synthesize frames that facilitate subsequent generation, leading to visual drift and structural collapse as rollouts extend. To address this limitation, we propose Hindsight Forcing, which allows historical chunks to learn directly from future outcomes by decoupling forward generation from backward credit assignment via a latent straight-through bridge. In the forward pass, each chunk completes a full multi-step rollout to update the KV cache. In the backward pass, the bridge routes gradients from future losses back to a single selected denoising step per historical chunk, training both the context writer and historical denoiser on shared parameters without retaining the full trajectory graph. Remarkably, Hindsight Forcing requires no additional model parameters, architecture modifications, or separate trajectory replay. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that Hindsight Forcing outperforms existing baselines in overall visual quality and dynamic motion, while ablation studies validate the benefit of supervising historical denoising. Code is available at https://github.com/haonanAN309/Hindsight-Forcing.

title: $R^2$: Recognizing and Reducing Redundant Visual Tool Use
summary: Recent studies have shown that visual tools can improve multimodal reasoning. However, the effects of tools vary substantially across samples, and benchmark accuracy alone does not reveal whether tool interactions are beneficial or redundant. We present $R^2$, a framework that recognizes and reduces redundant visual tool use in vision-language models. We first introduce a sample-level Category Analysis of Tool Utility (CAT), which categorizes samples according to whether a model can benefit from tools. This analysis reveals that benchmark scores may obscure a model's tool-use ability. Across seven benchmarks, samples benefiting from tools account for at most 12.44% of each benchmark, while the majority gain little from tool interaction or are even harmed by it. To assess individual calls, we propose the Visual Feedback Dependency (VFD) metric, which compares the likelihood of the same subsequent reasoning under actual and alternative visual feedback without an external evaluator or trajectory regeneration. Redundancy-Aware GRPO (RA-GRPO) combines this dependency signal with a category-conditioned base call cost to assign relative efficiency advantages among correct trajectories, supplementing outcome-based supervision. Across the seven benchmarks, RA-GRPO reduces the mean number of tool calls by 12.39% relative to Vanilla GRPO at comparable benchmark accuracy. Evaluated by tool-utility category, RA-GRPO improves category macro-average accuracy over Vanilla GRPO by 3.35 percentage points.

title: Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. The last mile, step-level credit, usually requires step labels, a learned critic, costly LLM judges or hand-written rules. We introduce DM-PRM, which turns a general-purpose decision model -- one answering yes/no questions with probabilities -- into a general-purpose process reward model (PRM), zero-shot: no step labels, no fine-tuning, no critic. DM-PRM asks one question per step and adds the standardised answers to the advantage. It plugs into any policy-gradient method; one model, with one question text per environment, serves household tasks, web shopping and multiple RL methods. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it lifts GRPO by over twenty points on ALFWorld and over ten on WebShop, overtakes GiGPO on ALFWorld and learns in far fewer iterations; it also improves GiGPO and GraphGPO on both benchmarks and reaches the highest success of our comparison, ahead of critic-based PPO and of state-of-the-art GiGPO, HGPO and GraphGPO. Its scores locate useful steps in failed rollouts, and trained agents drop idle actions and explore instead of circling. DM-PRM shows that step credit need not be learned: it can be asked for.

title: Online Learning for Minimizing Maximum Tardiness in Single-Machine Scheduling
comment: Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)
summary:
We study online learning for minimizing maximum tardiness (\OMMT) in single-machine scheduling. In each round, the learner selects a permutation of \(n\) fixed jobs, representing a schedule. The environment then reveals a processing time and a due date for each job, and the learner incurs a vector-valued loss whose components correspond to the tardiness of the individual jobs. The goal of the learner is to minimize \(α\)-regret, the difference between the learner's maximum cumulative tardiness and \(α\) times that of the best fixed permutation in hindsight, for as small \(α\) as possible. We investigate OMMT under both stochastic and adversarial environments. In the stochastic setting, we prove that the expected \(1\)-regret of the Follow-the-Leader (FTL) algorithm is \(
  O\!\left(\frac{n\log n}{Δ^2}\right) \), together with a corresponding high-probability bound, where \(Δ\) is a distribution-dependent gap parameter. At round \(t \in \{1,\dots,T\}\), FTL runs in \(O(tn^2)\) time and \(O(tn)\) space. In the adversarial setting, we prove that, for any \(0<c<\log_2 n/16\), the \(α\)-regret is \(Ω(T)\) whenever \(α<\log_2 n/16-c\). We then reduce OMMT to a surrogate online learning problem and apply Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL), obtaining an expected \(α\)-regret bound of \(O(n^2\sqrt{T})\) for \(α=O(\log n)\). Thus, the logarithmic dependence of \(α\) on \(n\) is tight up to constant factors. Each FTPL update admits a mixed-integer programming formulation whose size is polynomial in \(n\) and \(t\).

title: COMPASS: Cross-modal Observation with Multi-Path Adaptive Stopping and Selection for Early Time Series Classification
summary: Early time-series classification (ETSC) balances predictive performance against the amount of observed data. In multimodal settings, modality-associated and fused branches may differ in predictive ability at the same observed prefix, motivating joint decisions about when to stop and which branch should provide the final prediction. We propose COMPASS, a two-stage framework that preserves two modality-associated temporal branches and one fusion branch. The first stage combines cross-modal feature exchange and gated fusion with branch-wise supervision at every prefix. The second stage optimizes a shared four-action controller to continue observation or terminate through one of the frozen branches. Experiments on six physiological and wearable datasets compare COMPASS with multimodal adaptations of five ETSC baselines. COMPASS achieves the best average ranks in accuracy-earliness harmonic mean, AUROC, and earliness within this comparison set. At identical learned stopping times, branch selection improves mean accuracy over fusion readout on five of the six datasets, with gains of 2.35 and 2.16 percentage points on ISRUC-Sleep and UCDDB, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on joint stopping and branch selection for multimodal early time series classification.

title: Dynamic Token Merging for Efficient Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent each image with hundreds of visual tokens, which can make inference costly even when a prompt depends on only part of the image. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), introduced in MrT5 for byte-level text encoders, learns which tokens to remove: a lightweight delete gate scores contextualized hidden states, acts as a differentiable attention bias during training, and physically removes tokens at inference. We argue that DTM is a general token deletion framework rather than a byte-level technique, and extend it to the vision modality and to decoder-only models. Applying DTM to T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 yields V-MrT5Gemma2, which deletes visual tokens inside a bidirectional multimodal encoder, and V-MrGemma3, which compacts the prompt and its key-value caches during decoder-only prefill. Across ten benchmarks, DTM's advantage over attention-based and random deletion grows with the deletion rate and is largest on document, chart, and scene-text reading. At 80% visual token deletion (approximately 60% fewer FLOPs), DTM raises accuracy over FastV from 51.8 to 63.0 on ChartQA and from 63.3 to 67.8 on TextVQA with V-MrT5Gemma2, as well as from 62.2 to 68.8 and from 71.2 to 75.1 with V-MrGemma3, retaining 90-96% of unpruned performance on both tasks with significant efficiency gains. These results support DTM as a general framework for efficient transformers.

title: V2VFusion: Text-Controlled Video-to-Video Diffusion for Degradation-Aware Video Fusion
summary: Video fusion integrates complementary information in multiple source video streams into a single sequence for complete scene perception. Existing methods perform frame-wise fusion and lack unified spatio-temporal modeling across sequences, damaging temporal coherence across sequences. When dealing with degradations, they also ignore temporal dynamics and overload a single network with diverse degradations, leading to limited and imbalanced degradation suppression. To address these issues, we propose V2VFusion, the first unified video-to-video fusion framework that directly generates temporally coherent, high-quality fused videos from degraded multi-source inputs. By reformulating video fusion as a video-to-video conditional generation problem in latent diffusion space, our approach holistically models spatio-temporal dependencies across entire sequences and intrinsically ensures sequence-level consistency. On this basis, a text-guided degradation-conditioned ControlNet bridges high-level textual degradation descriptions with low-level visual priors, enabling interpretable and controllable guidance for structure-preserving fusion beyond purely data-driven conditioning. To handle heterogeneous and compound degradations, a state-modulated degradation-aware hierarchical mixture-of-experts module decouples expert selection into diffusion-state-aware filtering and degradation-aware routing. It prevents unreliable routing and fosters expert specialization to mitigate representation conflicts among diverse degradations. Experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, and multi-focus video fusion tasks and complex degradations validate that V2VFusion surpasses existing methods in fusion quality and temporal stability. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenDoubleJ/V2VFusion.

title: Rethinking Cross-Sensor Domain Adaptation for Bridge Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation
summary: Segmentation models for bridge point clouds lose accuracy when trained on terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) data and applied to mobile laser scanning (MLS) data. This study re-examines the SemanticBridge TLS-to-MLS protocol to determine how sampling density, surface roughness, color, and acquisition viewpoint are expressed in the 8-cm sparse-voxel representation, and how adaptation gains depend on source-model convergence. Using one sparse-convolution U-Net, we combine raw-point statistics with controlled input perturbations and compare adaptive batch normalization, entropy minimization, Mean Teacher, and confidence-filtered self-training under 100- and 300-epoch schedules. TLS and MLS have similar nearest-neighbor spacing after preprocessing (12.08 and 12.02 mm), and a 4-mm perturbation of TLS points changes voxel occupancy by only 4.4%. Color distributions differ systematically, but zeroing color on identical voxels changes target mean intersection over union (mIoU) by only +0.02, and by +0.06 after the color augmentation is scale-corrected. The sensors also observe different portions of the bridge, yielding different class proportions. A 300-epoch source-only model obtains 57.80 mIoU on the paired-bridge protocol. Confidence-filtered self-training improves the 100-epoch baseline, but from a converged model it changes target mIoU by -0.97 (source-selected checkpoints) and -2.44 (final-50-epoch means). Repeated evaluation (standard deviation 0.27-0.64) and seed variation (1.88 across three seeds) are comparable to several method differences. Adaptation results on this benchmark therefore depend on representation scale, source-model convergence, and evaluation variability.

title: Structural Agreement Indicates Prediction Accuracy For Protein-Ligand Co-Folding
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 20 supplementary figures, 3 supplementary tables. Code: https://github.com/oxpig/core-score
summary: Co-folding models predict the structures of proteins and their bound ligands, but their accuracy varies across targets. Their usefulness therefore depends on knowing which predictions a user can trust. Confidence scores are intended to guide that choice. However, across seven co-folding models, we show that confidence-based selection offers little improvement over choosing a prediction at random. For approximately three-quarters of structures, predictions are either exclusively correct or incorrect, leaving no opportunity for ranking to change the outcome. Moreover, high confidence does not reliably discriminate correct top-ranked predictions from incorrect ones. We find that structural agreement among predictions is a more accurate measure of likely success than current confidence scores. We capture this with the Concentration of Repeated Ensembles (CORE) Score, which combines cluster tightness with ensemble support. CORE Score discriminates top-1 success and oracle success, achieving mean ROC AUCs of 0.866 and 0.838, compared to 0.757 and 0.759 for ipTM. CORE Score also outperforms training set similarity measures, including ligand Tanimoto, protein sequence, and Runs N' Poses similarity, despite requiring no experimental ligand pose. Structural agreement is therefore a practical indicator of reliability and a baseline for evaluating future confidence estimators, without requiring an additional trained uncertainty estimator.

title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks
summary: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.

title: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training
summary: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.

title: Towards Text-Mask Consistency in Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Vision-language models for medical image segmentation often produce masks that conflict with the accompanying text, especially under multi-site/multi-lesion descriptions. We trace this failure to two factors: (i) highly templated and repetitive clinical language causes one-to-one hard contrastive learning to yield numerous false negatives, weakening cross-modal alignment; and (ii) predominantly vision-driven, one-way cross-attention lacks a language-dominant, spatially aware pathway, hindering effective injection of textual semantics into the spatial visual domain. To this end, we propose Consistency-enhanced Two-stage Segmentation (C2Seg). In the pretraining stage, Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning uses a frozen strong baseline to construct an intra-batch text similarity matrix as soft labels, thereby alleviating false negative conflicts and producing more discriminative visual representations. In the fusion stage, we introduce a Bidirectional Complementary Attention Module, where each modality dominates attention along its own path, fostering deep interaction and structural consistency between visual and textual representations. In order to enhance the expressive power of multimodal features, we further adopt KAN-based Attention Gating. Without updating the language encoder, our approach significantly improves text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/C2Seg.

title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: Stateful Privacy Sniffing of LLM Agents via Behavioral Covert Channels in Web Interactions
summary:
LLM agents increasingly rely on Web interaction, issuing searches, following links, and reading pages, to complete complex user tasks. Since each action is driven by the agent's private context, including the user's prompt, dialogue history, memory, and connected data, it also opens a new privacy exposure surface. Prior attacks either passively analyze network traffic, which yields only coarse correlations, or hijack the agent through indirect prompt injection, which must place sensitive content in an outgoing field and is blocked by content-level defenses. Whether an attacker can actively recover fine-grained private context without any explicit transmission thus remains insufficiently understood.
  Our insight is that an agent's benign Web decisions themselves leak private context, as what it chooses to visit encodes whether, which, and in what order it acts, forming a behavioral covert channel. Building on this, we design SNOOP, a stateful hierarchical probing framework that narrows a coarse-to-fine hypothesis tree per task and reconstructs user queries and profiles from the agent's observable paths. Across four agents and three LLM backbones on 500 StackExchange queries and 378 multi-turn iKAT dialogues, SNOOP recovers query concepts with an average F1 of 0.89 and user profiles with an F1 of 0.80, while four representative agent defenses change its recovery by less than 0.03 F1. Since no sensitive content is ever transmitted, content-level inspection cannot detect this leakage; we therefore propose Selection-Obfuscated Retrieval (SOR), which acquires resources under a fixed budget independent of private context and confines the agent's selection to a local snapshot, cutting SNOOP's F1 to 0.39 without additional LLM inference.

title: Action-Conditioned Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
summary: We study spatio-temporal forecasting in networked systems under specified actions. The challenge is to capture the action's effects without predicting spurious changes in unaffected regions. However, direct supervision and evaluation of these effects require paired futures with and without the action, whereas observational trajectories reveal only the realized future. We introduce PairST, a benchmark comprising six datasets across traffic, power transmission and water distribution, with paired reference and intervened futures simulated from the same system state. These pairs enable separate evaluation of affected-region forecast accuracy and quiet-region response error. We further propose ActionST, which forecasts the intervened future by writing an explicit response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast. Specifically, node-time addressing constructs a query for each response position, a state-conditioned response writer computes candidate responses, and a graph-aware locality gate controls their strength. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ActionST at new action targets, with the lowest mean absolute error on five datasets and the best average rank. Our source code and the PairST benchmark are available at https://github.com/yutong-xia/ActionST.

title: Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced Hierarchy-Aware Semi-Supervised Graph Classification
summary: Semi-supervised graph classification aims to learn graph-level representations by leveraging a large number of unlabeled graphs alongside a small set of labeled ones, effectively mitigating the issue of label scarcity. Despite significant progress by various semi-supervised learning strategies, complex relationships among graph vertices beyond pairwise edges, especially hierarchical structures, remain underexplored by existing methods. In this work, we propose a Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced hierarchy-aware framework, namely HypSEE, for semi-supervised graph classification. Specifically, we first construct walk-induced and embedding-derived hypergraphs to capture hierarchy-aware local and long-range higher-order relationships within graphs. Then, we devise a hierarchical hypergraph pooling approach guided by hypergraph structural entropy (HSE) to facilitate hierarchical representation learning in hypergraphs. Lastly, we employ an anchor graph-based consistency strategy to mutually align the representations from these two hypergraph views, enhancing the learning efficacy on unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on 8 benchmark datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our approach.

title: Disentangling Verbalized Evaluation Awareness and Refusal through Neuron-Level Intervention
summary: As large reasoning models (LRMs) become more capable, reliable evaluation becomes essential. LRMs can sometimes recognize that they are being evaluated, a phenomenon known as \emph{evaluation awareness}. This phenomenon raises concerns about whether safety behavior, particularly refusal behavior, generalizes from evaluation to deployment. Prior work manipulates \emph{verbalized evaluation awareness (VEA)} through activation steering and observes higher refusal rates when VEA is present, but the mechanisms underlying this connection remain poorly understood. We identify \emph{VEA neurons} by contrasting their activations in VEA and non-VEA reasoning segments. Intervening on 5,000 VEA neurons reduces the VEA rate from 12.6--51.8\% to at most 1.4\% across the model benchmark combinations in our main experiments, and lowers a probe score for unverbalized evaluation awareness (unVEA). In QwQ-32B, VEA-neuron intervention also reduces refusal even in rollouts without VEA; VEA text itself explains only 4--10\% of the decrease. We further show that their down-projection vectors contain refusal components, and preserving these components during intervention partially restores refusal while maintaining VEA suppression, accounting for about half of the refusal decrease and providing a mechanistic explanation for the connection between evaluation awareness and refusal. Finally, across the OLMo 3 SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints, the VEA rate on SorryBench and StrongREJECT is similar after SFT and DPO but substantially higher after RLVR, alongside an increase in the number of VEA neurons. Together, these findings show that VEA text itself has a limited effect on refusal, and that VEA neurons integrate evaluation awarenss and refusal.

title: TSIR: Ray-Traced Triangle Splats for Inverse Rendering
summary: Inverse rendering enables realistic relighting for visual effects and augmented reality. However, overlapping Gaussian primitives complicate surface recovery and require costly multi-layer traversal and compositing for light transport. We propose TSIR, a two-stage inverse rendering method that reconstructs relightable triangle splats from multi-view images. The first stage prepares opaque triangle splats with learnable vertex shading normals. The second stage directly traces these surfaces to estimate materials through Monte Carlo integration of direct illumination and indirect reflections, reducing reliance on multi-layer compositing. Anti-aliasing improves rendering quality while maintaining efficiency. Experiments demonstrate higher relighting quality than the evaluated baselines and more efficient anti-aliasing than supersampling.

title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics
summary: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.

title: Toward a digital twin of the ICU patient: Forecasting and treatment response in a generative event model
summary: A digital twin of a patient in intensive care would forecast the patient's course and what a treatment would change. Generative event models, trained to continue a patient's electronic health record (EHR), have been proposed as a path toward such twins. We trained TWICE, a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer, on the ICU records of one academic health system (127,332 training patients and 1.57 billion tokens). We evaluated it on clinical prediction tasks, generation fidelity, individual trajectories and counterfactual validation. Reading 19 clinical outcomes off 50 simulated futures, with no task-specific training, TWICE matched the best of 144 supervised configurations on held-out patients (mean AUROC 0.836 vs. 0.834). It led on events that change care within a day and trailed on death. With the training data fixed, more and longer simulated futures were worth more than a 6.8-fold larger model. Its generated records matched real ones closely and were as specific to each patient as its own variability allowed. Its predicted risk rose as events approached. Pre-specified controls showed that it reproduced the side effects of drugs and was barely moved by an inert drug. On the values that treatments are given to correct, however, an opposite treatment moved its forecasts like the right one. TWICE forecasts ICU events about as well as task-specific models, and we see it as a step toward a digital twin of the ICU patient.

title: ReactDrive: Self-Reactive Driving World Model
summary: The world evolves through the dynamics of its constituent entities and their interactions, with changes in one entity influencing the behavior of others. To simulate this evolution under different actions, interactive world models need to capture the resulting agent responses as part of the world's own dynamics. In autonomous driving, errors in modeling these responses can misrepresent maneuver safety and undermine the reliability of generated videos used for policy evaluation and learning. To formalize this intrinsic requirement for driving world model, we define self-reactivity as the capability to model agent responses from observed history and a specified ego action, and generate visual futures that reflect those responses without prescribed future agent trajectories. To realize this capability, we introduce ReactDrive, a driving world model that jointly learns agent dynamics and visual generation through a shared agent state representation. Within this framework, dynamics supervision grounds a reactive dynamics prior in observed agent states, while the video objective jointly optimizes the self-reactivity and visual realism. Experiments show improved agent responses, ego controllability, and video quality, a 96.0% preference for agent reactivity in human comparisons across five baselines, and better downstream planning through augmentation with generated videos. We hope this work encourages the community to recognize self-reactivityas a foundational capability for developing and evaluating interactive world models. Project page: https://reactdrive.github.io/ .

title: Integral Multipliers and Arithmetic Obstructions for Two-Hidden-Layer ReLU Maxima
summary: We study exact representations of maximum functions by ReLU networks with two hidden layers and integer parameters. The least positive output multiplier is two for the six-input maximum, and either two or six for the seven-input maximum. We obtain these bounds from integral cubical fillings and a coefficient-preserving passage from polytope identities to networks. For the coordinate-facet complex of the six-simplex, we compute a coning index of six over the integers and three after inverting two, allowing arbitrary integral directions within each facet. A class in the homology of the unrestricted kernel complex characterizes the remaining seven-input problem; its vanishing is equivalent to an integral filling of a fixed target. We also construct a finite character that separates rational from three-local representability in a dictionary containing two known constructions and all pairs of edge-disjoint three-edge forests. This obstruction permits nonsymmetric coefficients and is confined to the specified dictionary. Control of lower-dimensional remainders yields a sufficient criterion in the top-dimensional quotient. Exact certificates and verification programs accompany the finite calculations.

title: Real-Time On-Drone Hyperspectral Anomaly Detection for Wilderness Search and Rescue
summary: Wilderness search-and-rescue (WSAR) teams use uncrewed aerial systems (UASs) to survey terrain for indicators of missing persons that are rare, blend into the background, or lack thermal signatures. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) provides rich spectral information, but its high data volume challenges real-time on-drone processing. We present SABL, an edge-computing pipeline for on-drone Spectral Anomaly-Based Localization. SABL integrates hyperspectral streaming with exponentially moving Reed-Xiaoli (ERX) anomaly detection and DBSCAN spatial filtering to group pixel-level anomalies into candidate search regions. SABL is evaluated on data collected during a 10-day deployment with Quinhagak Search and Rescue (QSAR) in remote Alaska. It processes hyperspectral scanlines at 5.67-5.73 ms per line, meeting the camera's 10-ms acquisition interval; DBSCAN requires only 6.5-12.5 ms per 100-line update for filtering. SABL achieves approximately 56% and 99% object-level precision on QSAR-selected search indicators across two scenes, with corresponding recall of 55% and 29%, providing significant background filtering while identifying difficult-to-see anomalous search indicators.

title: Same Facts, Different Decision: Fact-Invariant Manipulation and Provenance-Based Defense in Typed Decision Models
summary: Typed decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer only with a probability, an option, or a score, so software can act on them directly. Their inputs, however, often include text from outsiders. Prior attacks test this risk poorly. Injected instructions rarely work on these models, and added facts can make a changed decision correct. We show that outside comments can persuade these models to make a wrong decision without adding any fact. We propose LEVER, an attack that writes such comments with four levers from argumentation theory, uses a separate verifier to discard any comment that adds a fact, and searches for effective comments guided by the model's output probabilities. We further propose the Provenance Gate, a defense that accepts a changed decision only if the model reaches it again without the outside comments. On three benchmarks, LEVER flips about a third of Jev's correct decisions, 2.8 times as many as the strongest prior attack under the same limit on facts, and more on five other models. The gate blocks all of these attacks with at most one extra query and still accepts trusted updates.

title: Ruby: State-of-the-Art Potency Prediction across Discovery Regimes Using Learned Structural Representations
summary: Small-molecule drug discovery proceeds through repeated design-make-test-analyze cycles. The goal is often to maximize potency while keeping other properties within the ranges required for a viable therapeutic candidate. Compound prioritization places different demands on computational methods as drug discovery progresses from hit identification through hit-to-lead and lead optimization, with changing computational budgets and increasing amounts of on-target experimental data. We introduce Ruby, a Robust Universal Binding affinitY predictor that uses intermediate representations from the structural foundation model Pearl without requiring an explicit binding pose for every compound. Ruby is trained on proprietary data plus GenesisPotency-2026, an audited public-source potency training dataset released for academic and commercial use under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license with row-level provenance and audit annotations. Ruby achieves the highest aggregate early enrichment across seven public hit-identification targets among evaluated methods, with adjustable inference effort trading off enrichment and computational cost over more than two orders of magnitude. Ruby achieves the highest average correlations across four public benchmarks: OpenFE, CASP16, FEP+ 4, and OpenBind. Ruby significantly outperforms other methods in zero-shot prediction across eight biochemical and cellular assays from five ongoing Genesis-Incyte programs, widening its performance advantage relative to the public benchmarks. Ruby continues to improve more than other methods when all are given the opportunity to recalibrate using earlier assay measurements. Together, these contributions provide an annotated training resource for the field and a state-of-the-art potency predictor for broad screening, prioritization within related chemical series, and assay-specific prediction as experimental measurements accumulate.

title: Many Plans at Once: Diverse Top-Quality Planning in Continuous Time
summary: Planners for physical systems usually return a single trajectory, which leaves no alternative when an unmodeled constraint invalidates the chosen route or downstream preferences change. A set of plans computed in advance provides ready-made alternatives and warm-starts for fast adaptation, but only if the plans are both low-cost and mutually distinct. Discrete planning addresses this with top-quality and diverse planning, but these ideas do not transfer to continuous time, where every valid trajectory has infinitely many valid near-copies, and existing trajectory planners converge to one or a few solutions. We present Many Plans at Once (MPAO), which treats every plan it finds as a reason to search elsewhere: it samples untrained neural networks whose outputs meet the boundary conditions by construction, trains corrections shared by networks from the same distribution, stores every validated plan, and adapts its sampling to what it has found, which makes it anytime. We define the goal by bringing the cost bound of top-quality planning and the distinctness threshold of diverse planning to continuous time. Under equal budgets against five baselines, MPAO is the only method that solves all 40 instances across four domains. On contact-rich manipulation, it is the only method with plans within 25% of the best known cost on one task, and returns about ten times as many such plans as the strongest baseline on the other two.

title: Fair Property Tax: Reducing Regressivity in Machine-Learning Valuation
summary: Advanced machine-learning models are increasingly used for property valuation in tax assessment. Although these models can achieve high predictive accuracy, they may systematically assign higher valuation-to-sale ratios to lower-priced properties, a pattern known as regressivity. In collaboration with the Cook County Assessor's Office (CCAO), we develop and evaluate two training methods that substantially reduce this regressive pattern while maintaining price-scale predictive accuracy. The Direct method has been incorporated into CCAO's public residential valuation software. Retaining the LightGBM model class used at CCAO, we propose a Direct penalty on squared covariance between log valuation errors and log sale prices, and an observation-additive Surrogate that yields a weighted squared-error loss. We evaluate both methods in our implementation of the CCAO workflow, using seven chronological validation folds, a held-out test set, and a 2025-forward test set. Measured by the magnitude of price-related bias (PRB), regressivity falls by approximately 49% on held-out sales and 39% on 2025 sales at a Surrogate setting selected by cross-validation, relative to the same LightGBM model fitted without the penalty. Price-scale $R^2$ is essentially unchanged. Its small rise, from 0.893 to 0.897 on held-out sales and from 0.904 to 0.908 on 2025 sales, reflects overall valuation level. Log-price RMSE rises by 3.1% and 1.7%, respectively. Paired sale-bootstrap 90% intervals for the PRB reductions lie within about two percentage points of these estimates. In an additional eight-county benchmark, both methods reduce regressivity in every county, with higher log-price prediction error as the expected tradeoff. These findings demonstrate a practical way to reduce measured regressivity within an existing assessor workflow while preserving price-scale predictive performance.

title: Scalable Evaluation of Medical AI using Evidence-based Practice Recommendations
summary: Rigorously evaluating medical artificial intelligence (AI) requires testing open-ended clinical management across diverse presentations and stages of care. However, existing benchmarks rely on manual expert authoring, limiting coverage across conditions, conditional care pathways, and evolving guidelines. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts and verifies structured clinical criteria and branching decision trees from practice recommendations to generate scenarios spanning the care continuum, including nuanced presentations and practice variations across regions and guideline editions. Applied to 436 BMJ Best Practice clinical monographs (354 US, 82 International), this yields 3,200 scenarios spanning differential diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications, plus targeted suites for regional specificity (731 US/International pairs) and temporal freshness (630 scenarios). To grade responses, we develop a clinician-calibrated autorater that scores management plans on a 4-point rubric stratifying deviations by clinical severity. Across Gemini models, scaling improves adherence, while web search (+0.8 percentage points [pp] on average) and multi-sample synthesis (+2.2 pp) combine additively (+2.8 pp). In context, full monographs consistently trail condensed excerpts. On targeted suites, web search narrows international performance gaps (+4.2 pp) and improves adherence to newly updated guidance (+4.6 pp). In a study with Primary Care Physicians (n = 9) across 200 scenarios, AI assistance raises adherence from 50.5% to 70.0%, driven largely by fewer clinical omissions. Overall, our results demonstrate a scalable evaluation setup using an evidence-based corpus originally written to guide human clinical decision-making, and demonstrate its viability to assess medical AI and its assistance on clinician decision-making.

title: S2D-Splat: Static-First Gaussian Reconstruction of Dynamic Driving Scenes with Layer-Wise Feature Guidance
summary: Moving objects introduce cross-frame inconsistencies that complicate camera estimation and static geometry recovery in driving scenes. Recent feed-forward Gaussian methods explicitly separate static and dynamic primitives, but often estimate camera parameters and geometry from shared features that jointly encode both components, leaving static reconstruction susceptible to dynamic interference. To address this challenge, we propose S2D-Splat, a feed-forward framework for static-first Gaussian reconstruction with layer-wise feature guidance. Our framework separates static and dynamic features before camera and geometry estimation, enabling the static branch to recover camera parameters and static 3D Gaussians with reduced dynamic interference. Intermediate static features are cached at each layer and reused as fixed conditioning at corresponding layers of the dynamic branch. This asymmetric information flow preserves the established static representations while providing stable geometric context for reconstructing dynamic 3D Gaussians. An instance-level motion decoder further queries the fused static and dynamic representations to estimate object trajectories, supporting motion-aligned Gaussian fusion and temporal interpolation. Experiments on Waymo and zero-shot evaluations on nuScenes and the MM-AU accident dataset demonstrate that S2D-Splat outperforms existing approaches on most evaluated metrics and generalizes to highly dynamic, pre-collision driving scenarios.

title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model
summary: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. Second, the language decision model (e.g., \jev{}) reads these indicators together with the customer's profile and activity, judges the case in context with broad world knowledge, and returns the score of high risk. We evaluate JevRisk on the anti-money laundering task with public synthetic data from Scotiabank and on the credit risk task with real data from Home Credit and Lending Club. On both tasks, JevRisk outperforms rule-based and unsupervised methods, and is on par with or better than supervised methods (e.g., GBDT and TabPFN) trained on about a thousand labelled customers.

title: Reward Integrity in Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for LLM Guardrail Red-Teaming
comment: Received the Best Paper Award at the Reinforcement Learning for LLM Agents Workshop at ACM International Conference for AI in Finance 2026 in Milan
summary: We study reward fidelity in an adversarial reinforcement-learning loop for red-teaming financial-services language-model guardrails. Apparent wins can arise when an attack omits prescribed personally identifiable information (PII), or when a reward judge credits a response that did not break the targeted policy. On attacker-generated and public benchmark examples, TypeSafe Jev checks whether the prescribed PII is present. For outcome scoring, we compare the decision models TypeSafe Jev, Laya (pretrained and post-trained), and pretrained CLM-8B with logged Opus 4.8 judgements from a replay corpus. Post-training markedly improves Laya's agreement with the judge. A separate author-reviewed off-target set establishes that Opus can award false wins. The findings motivate specialised decision-model judges for checking prescribed PII in attack inputs and scoring target responses against the intended policy.

title: SceneRuler: Measuring Physical Quantities in Video via Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction
summary: Many questions about videos ask for a number, such as how tall a person is, how far a cart travels, or how fast a ball leaves a ramp. We study this task, quantitative physical reasoning from video, where the inputs are a video, a question, and a prior of known facts such as object sizes, speeds, and distances from the camera to named objects. End-to-end video-language models lack an explicit metric scale and physical consistency, and their errors cannot be inspected. We present SceneRuler, which instead recovers a measurable physical scene and answers with that scene as evidence. Its central principle, Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction, builds, for each question, only the smallest scene that suffices to measure the asked quantity, and tests sufficiency on measurements rather than assuming it. The scene is written as a program whose structure a vision-language model writes and whose magnitudes are left to measurement. Physics-guided Fitting measures them through physical motion laws, so that gravity itself can anchor the metric scale, and marks every parameter, and the read-out of the asked quantity, as determined or undetermined. Each question receives a read-out and an answer. The read-out is the asked quantity evaluated on the scene, and it is empty when the scene does not fix that quantity. The answer is always given by a model that takes the scene as evidence. We evaluate on QuantiPhy and also apply the method to 27 in-the-wild videos that we collected, which have no ground-truth answers. On its validation split, the final answer reaches a mean relative accuracy of 0.709 against 0.624 for the strongest baseline, and the reconstruction determines the asked quantity on 47 of 158 questions, where the final answer reaches 0.781. Because every intermediate quantity is explicit, each answer can be traced to the objects, scale, and motion behind it.

title: From Letter-of-Credit Requirements to Executable Specifications: Evaluating Verification Accuracy and Completeness
comment: Accepted at the 3rd Workshop on LLMs and Generative AI for Finance (AI4F) at ACM ICAIF 2026 (non-archival). 10 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Code: https://github.com/Ji-S/LC-Spec-Synth
summary: In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was examined. We therefore evaluate examination requirement by requirement and make each requirement executable. A language model converts the bill of lading (BL) and commercial invoice (IV) requirements of a credit into atomic conditions and logical structures, and a deterministic verifier retrieves the named evidence and computes each outcome, so every check can be compared with a gold encoding and traced to logged evidence. Because LC records are confidential, our on-premises 9B parser is fine-tuned only on synthetic pairs built from templates and human-reviewed public document values. On 345 real LC cases, final-decision accuracy proves misleading: a constant PASS rule has the highest raw accuracy while examining nothing. Although it never sees a real record during training, the fine-tuned parser detects 93% of the atomic requirements its ontology covers and reconstructs 86% of the covered requirements exactly. It verifies 82% of the evaluable requirements correctly, against 54% for a tool-using agent, and leads the agent on both satisfied requirements and discrepancies. It also completely examines 1.8 times as many cases as few-shot prompting of the same model, while direct prediction and the agent complete none. Executing the gold encodings with the same verifier shows that some of the remaining errors, missed discrepancies included, come from the operators and normalization, which a better parser alone cannot fix. Every rejection comes with a trace of the units and evidence behind it, which suits examiner-in-the-loop review.

title: Distributional Algebro-Geometric Persistence (dAGP): Wasserstein-Stable Polynomial-Relation Signatures
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Geometric Distributional Deep Learning (GDDL)
summary: A circle and a quartic superellipse have the same homology, but their defining equations have degrees two and four, respectively. We study this algebraic distinction for point-cloud distributions. For a probability measure $μ$ on $Ω=[-1,1]^d$ and an orthonormal polynomial feature map $φ_m$ of degree $m$, the moment matrix $G_m(μ)=\mathbb{E}_{X\simμ}[φ_m(X)φ_m(X)^\top]$ satisfies $c^\top G_m(μ)c=\mathbb{E}_μ[f_c(X)^2]$, so coefficient directions associated with its small eigenvalues represent low-degree polynomials that nearly vanish on $μ$. Counting these near-relation directions across degree $m$ and the tolerance $\varepsilon$ gives a two-parameter integer signature. We call this representation distributional algebro-geometric persistence (dAGP), the population counterpart of the point-cloud algebro-geometric persistence (AGP) construction. For empirical measures, dAGP is the sample-normalised counterpart of point-cloud AGP. We also show that $μ\mapsto G_m(μ)$ is Lipschitz in the $1$-Wasserstein distance, so its ordered eigenvalues vary Lipschitz-continuously under transport of mass, while its threshold counts remain unchanged under perturbations satisfying a spectral-margin condition. We give an explicit support-localised Lipschitz constant and identify the regime in which the resulting guarantee is informative. Experimentally, the population noise-floor prediction agrees with the finite-sample mean to $0.1\%$, within sampling error. At a selected tolerance, relation onset orders the conic, quartic, and non-algebraic closed curves, while their count profiles distinguish them from the two-dimensional control. Calibration identifies an empirical tolerance range.
